Week five. Her younger sister Aditi arrived with a tiffin of idlis and found Jaya crying over a pile of tiny clothes. "Some days I don't even want to hold him," Jaya whispered. "What kind of mother says that?" Aditi sat down beside her. "A tired one who needs help. This isn't your fault." That afternoon Aditi took her to the doctor, who listened carefully, said this happens to many new parents and gets better with help, and arranged regular sessions with a counsellor.
Week nine. The nights were still hard. But when the baby grabbed her plait, Jaya laughed, and the dread came less often.

passage:
Dear Rosa,
The baby is three weeks old, and our flat in Kochi has never been this full. Kunal's aunts arrived the day we came home, and the advice hasn't stopped: swaddle her tighter, don't let her sleep on you, cover her feet, why is she crying again? Each comment made sense on its own, but together they left me feeling like I was failing an exam I never studied for. I started feeding her in the bedroom with the door shut, just to have one quiet corner.
Kunal's mother has been different. She cooks, folds the laundry and takes the baby while I shower. Yesterday she saw me struggling with burping and asked, "Would a tip help, or shall I just keep you company?" I nearly cried. I said a tip, please, and it worked.
I feel more like her mother every day.
Love,
Elizabeth

You asked how the first months went? Honestly, crowded. We stayed at my parents' house in Mysuru, and every afternoon someone new walked in. One aunt said the baby cried because I, as his mother, was eating the wrong things. Another lifted him out of my arms to show me the "right" way to hold him. I smiled and nodded, and then cried in the bathroom. I stopped trusting my own hands.
Kunal noticed before I said a word. He started telling visitors, kindly, "Evenings are best, and if you'd like to help, the dishes are right there." He'd whisper to me, "Manjula, you know him best." My Ammamma took over the cooking and never gave a tip unless I asked. Slowly the house got quieter. I slept a little. By the time we went home, I could settle him in a way nobody had taught me. That felt like mine.

qa.a: At Manjula's parents' house in Mysuru.

qa.a: Kunal set visiting times and pointed helpers to practical jobs like the dishes, which gave Manjula rest and room to learn her baby's needs.

qa.a: Manjula would likely have kept feeling watched and unsure, and might never have found her own way to settle the baby.
